questions.stem: What distinguishes a devaluation from a depreciation?
options: A devaluation is a deliberate policy decision; a depreciation is a market movement
A devaluation is larger than a depreciation
A devaluation applies to imports and a depreciation to exports
A devaluation is temporary and a depreciation permanent
questions.why: Devaluation and revaluation are only possible under a fixed or managed system. Use the right word for the system in the question.
whyNot: Size is not the distinction.
Both affect imports and exports.
Neither is inherently temporary.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the Marshall-Lerner condition?
options: The sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports must exceed 1
Export prices must rise faster than import prices
The exchange rate must be floating
Exports must exceed imports
questions.why: If the sum is less than 1, a depreciation makes the current account worse, because the higher import prices dominate.
whyNot: That is an improvement in the terms of trade.
The condition applies under any regime.
That is a trade surplus.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the J-curve effect?
options: The current account worsens immediately after a depreciation before improving as volumes respond
The current account improves immediately and then worsens
The exchange rate falls and then recovers to its original level
Export volumes rise immediately after a depreciation
questions.why: Contracts are already signed and supply chains fixed, so prices change while quantities do not.
whyNot: The J shape is worse first, better later.
It describes the current account, not the rate itself.
Volumes take time to respond, which is the whole point.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines capital flight?
options: A large and rapid outflow of financial capital, usually caused by loss of confidence
The relocation of a factory to another country
The emigration of skilled workers
A fall in a country's capital stock through depreciation
questions.why: It sharply increases the supply of the currency and causes a steep depreciation, and it is self-reinforcing.
whyNot: That is off-shoring or FDI.
That is the brain drain.
That is capital consumption.

questions.stem: A country's currency appreciates. What happens to its exports and imports?
options: Exports become dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home
Exports become cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home
Both exports and imports become cheaper
Neither is affected
questions.why: SPICED: Strong currency, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer.
whyNot: That is the effect of a depreciation.
They move in opposite directions.
Both prices change in the relevant currency.

questions.stem: Higher domestic interest rates have what effect on a floating exchange rate?
options: They attract capital inflows, raising demand for the currency, so it appreciates
They increase the supply of the currency, so it depreciates
They have no effect, because interest rates are domestic
They fix the rate at its current level
questions.why: This is the most immediate influence on a floating rate, which is why interest rates are used to support a currency.
whyNot: Inflows raise demand, not supply.
Capital flows respond directly to relative returns.
Interest rates influence the rate; they do not fix it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes purchasing power parity theory?
options: Exchange rates adjust over the long run so a given sum buys the same basket in every country
Exchange rates are fixed by relative interest rates
Exchange rates always equal the ratio of the two countries' GDPs
Exchange rates are determined by the trade balance alone
questions.why: Its limitations are that many goods and most services are not traded, and that short-run rates are dominated by capital flows.
whyNot: Interest rates are a separate influence.
GDP does not determine the rate.
The current account is one influence among several.

questions.stem: Why does supporting a currency deplete reserves while weakening it does not?
options: Supporting it requires buying your own currency with finite foreign reserves; weakening it accumulates reserves
Weakening a currency is prohibited by the IMF
Supporting a currency requires no intervention
Reserves are unlimited in both directions
questions.why: That asymmetry explains why defending an overvalued currency so often fails against a determined speculative attack.
whyNot: Intervention to weaken a currency is common.
It requires active buying of the currency.
Foreign reserves are finite; domestic currency can be created.

options: Import prices rise directly, giving cost-push inflation, and higher demand adds demand-pull pressure
It reduces the money supply
It lowers the price of imported inputs
It always reduces aggregate demand
questions.why: Reduced competition from imports also removes discipline on domestic producers' prices.
whyNot: It does not reduce the money supply.
It raises the price of imported inputs.
It raises AD through net exports.

questions.stem: Why might a depreciation fail to improve the current account even in the long run?
options: If the sum of the two elasticities remains below 1, the higher import bill dominates
Export volumes never respond to price
Import volumes never respond to price
Depreciation has no effect on prices
questions.why: Elasticities are higher in the long run than the short run, so the condition may fail immediately and hold later, but not always.
whyNot: They do respond, though with a lag.
They also respond, subject to the availability of substitutes.
It changes prices in both currencies directly.

questions.stem: Why is a strong argument against a fixed exchange rate the absence of automatic adjustment?
options: An overvalued peg must be corrected by deflating the domestic economy instead
Fixed rates cannot be defended at all
Fixed rates always cause inflation
Fixed rates prevent all trade
questions.why: Under a float, a current account deficit corrects itself as the currency falls; under a peg, the domestic economy must adjust.
whyNot: They can be defended with reserves and interest rates.
Fixed rates impose discipline against inflation.
They provide certainty for traders.

questions.stem: Why is competitive devaluation described as a negative-sum game?
options: Competitiveness is relative, so retaliation leaves relative rates unchanged and everyone with higher import prices
Devaluation raises every country's output permanently
Only the first country to devalue ever gains
Devaluation is illegal under WTO rules
questions.why: It also removes the pressure to raise productivity, which is the only durable source of competitiveness.
whyNot: Retaliation cancels the competitive gain while leaving the inflation.
Even the first mover's gain is eroded by retaliation and inflation.
Exchange rate policy is not directly governed by WTO rules.

questions.stem: For an import-dependent economy with few domestic substitutes, what follows about a depreciation?
options: Demand for imports is highly inelastic, so the Marshall-Lerner condition is unlikely to hold
Demand for imports is highly elastic, so the condition certainly holds
Import prices will not rise
Export volumes will rise proportionally more than import prices
questions.why: It would raise the import bill without much volume adjustment, which is a coherent economic argument for exchange rate stability in such an economy.
whyNot: Few substitutes means inelastic, not elastic, demand.
They rise directly with the depreciation.
There is no reason to expect that where imports are essential.

questions.stem: What effect does quantitative easing tend to have on a currency?
options: It depreciates it, by raising the money supply and lowering long-term interest rates
It appreciates it, by raising confidence
It fixes it against a basket of currencies
It has no exchange rate effect
questions.why: It is usually pursued for domestic reasons, with the currency effect a side effect, and it is criticised abroad as an indirect competitive devaluation.
whyNot: Both mechanisms point towards depreciation.
It is not a pegging mechanism.
The money supply and interest rate effects both move the rate.

questions.stem: Why does a depreciation have an ambiguous effect on the financial account?
options: Cheaper domestic assets attract investment, while a falling currency may signal weakness and prompt outflows
The financial account is unaffected by exchange rates
Only the current account responds to exchange rates
Foreign investors always gain from a depreciation
questions.why: The net effect depends on whether the movement is seen as a correction or as the start of a decline.
whyNot: Asset values and expected returns both change.
Both accounts respond.
Existing foreign holders lose value in their own currency.

questions.stem: Why does the growth effect of a depreciation depend on spare capacity?
options: With no spare capacity, higher export demand produces inflation rather than extra output
Spare capacity determines the exchange rate
Export demand does not respond to prices
Capacity has no effect on the price level
questions.why: The AD/AS framework makes this explicit: a rightward shift in AD near full capacity raises prices more than output.
whyNot: Capacity does not determine the rate.
Export demand does respond, with a lag.
Capacity constraints are what make demand inflationary.
